checks.claim: Space Shuttle had three main engines (RS-25) burning liquid hydrogen with liquid oxygen
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'three RS-25 engines were mounted on the orbiter's aft end', 'liquid hydrogen as fuel and liquid oxygen as oxidizer'. NASA: 'Each Space Shuttle consisted of three Space Shuttle Main Engines', burning for 8.5 minutes after launch, i.e. all the way to main-engine cutoff. 'Rode into orbit on three main engines' leaves out the two solid rocket boosters (which gave most liftoff thrust) but does not deny them, so it stays true; optional polish: '...on three main engines, beside two solid boosters,'.

checks.claim: NASA engines page confirms three main engines, LH2/LOX, worked with the SRBs
Key: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O is balanced (4 H, 2 O each side); unbalanced H2 + O2 -> H2O has 2 O left, 1 O right
checks.note: Grokipedia uses this exact example: four hydrogen and two oxygen atoms each side.

checks.claim: Only coefficients may change; changing a subscript makes a different substance
checks.note: 'adjusting coefficients - never altering subscripts'; 'altering subscripts would represent a different substance'.

checks.claim: Wrong: H2 + O2 -> H2O2 (atoms even, but product is hydrogen peroxide, not water)
checks.note: H2 + O2 -> H2O2 is a real (direct-synthesis) reaction, but it is not the water-making reaction the stem asks to balance, and the context says exactly that. Correctly wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong: H2 + O2 -> 2H2O (H 2 vs 4)
checks.note: Arithmetic: unbalanced in hydrogen.

checks.claim: Wrong: 2H2 + 2O2 -> 2H2O (O 4 vs 2)
checks.note: Arithmetic: unbalanced in oxygen.

checks.claim: Context: no atom and no mass is made or lost (conservation of mass)
checks.note: 'the total mass of the reactants must equal the total mass of the products'.

checks.claim: Fritz Haber was a German chemist
checks.note: 'German physical chemist'.

checks.claim: Haber showed in 1909 how to join atmospheric nitrogen with hydrogen to make ammonia
checks.note: Lab demonstration with osmium in early/April 1909; 2 July 1909 run made 500-600 g of ammonia. Wikipedia agrees he first synthesised ammonia at lab scale.

checks.claim: Ammonia is the raw material of (nitrogen) fertiliser
Factories today pass the gases over hot iron, a catalyst, which is not used up
checks.note: Industrial catalyst is iron-based (magnetite with promoters, reduced to iron); 400-500 C. It deactivates slowly by poisoning/sintering and is replaced after years, but is not consumed by the reaction.

checks.claim: Key: N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3 (2 N, 6 H each side)
checks.note: Grokipedia: N2 + 3H2 <=> 2NH3.

checks.claim: Wrong: N2 + 3H2 -> NH3 (N 2 vs 1; H 6 vs 3)
checks.note: Arithmetic.

checks.claim: Wrong: N2 + 2H2 -> 3NH3 (N 2 vs 3; H 4 vs 9)
checks.note: Arithmetic.

checks.claim: Wrong: N2 + 6H2 -> 2NH3 (H 12 vs 6)
checks.note: Arithmetic; 'counting atoms instead of molecules' is a fair description of the slip.

checks.claim: Context: Haber's ammonia feeds about half the world's people
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'The food base of half the current world population is based on the Haber-Bosch process'; Grokipedia: 'an estimated 50% of the world's population'.

checks.claim: Context: 1918 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
checks.note: Prize for 1918, announced 1919, presented 1920; 'the 1918 Nobel Prize' is the correct name.

checks.claim: Context: Haber oversaw Germany's first great chlorine gas attack, at Ypres, April 1915
checks.note: Grokipedia: oversaw 'the first major deployment of chlorine gas' at Second Ypres, 22 April 1915; Wikipedia: present when Germany first released chlorine there. ('First great chlorine attack' is right: earlier German gas use, e.g. Bolimow, January 1915, was a tear agent, not chlorine.)

checks.claim: Context: called the father of chemical warfare
checks.note: Told as what he 'is called', which matches both sources.

checks.claim: Key: zinc in dilute hydrochloric acid gives hydrogen, which burns with a squeaky pop at a lit splint
checks.note: Lit splint test 'most commonly used to identify hydrogen ... distinctive squeaky pop'. RSC: 'Metal + acid -> salt + hydrogen', lit splint held at the tube's mouth.

checks.claim: Metal + acid -> salt + hydrogen; zinc, magnesium, iron react; the salt here is zinc chloride
checks.note: RSC names magnesium and zinc chlorides as the salts formed; Grokipedia Hydrogen names zinc and iron with dilute HCl or H2SO4.

checks.claim: Wrong: carbon dioxide (comes from acid on a carbonate such as marble; would put the splint out)
checks.note: CO2 is non-flammable and extinguishes a lit splint (the limewater test is the proper ID test, since other gases also put a splint out, but the context's claim is still true). Grokipedia Carbon_dioxide: nonflammable, made by acids on carbonates.

checks.claim: Wrong: oxygen (does not burn; relights a glowing splint)
checks.note: 'oxygen is not flammable', an oxidizer that supports burning. Glowing splint 'flares, and re-ignites' in concentrated oxygen (Wikipedia Splint). 'Only makes a glowing splint flare up' is a fair plain-words statement of its test.

checks.claim: Wrong: chlorine (not produced by zinc and HCl; does not pop)
checks.note: Metal + acid gives hydrogen, not chlorine; chlorine's test is bleaching damp litmus.

checks.claim: HCl is a strong acid and NaOH a strong base
Key: neutralisation makes a salt and water (HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O)
checks.note: 'HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) -> NaCl(aq) + H2O(l)'; net 'H+(aq) + OH-(aq) -> H2O(l)'.

checks.claim: Wrong: a salt and hydrogen gas
checks.note: Hydrogen comes from acid on a metal, not from acid on a base.

checks.claim: Wrong: chlorine gas and water
checks.note: The chloride stays as dissolved chloride ions in NaCl; no chlorine gas forms.

checks.claim: Wrong: a weaker acid and a weaker base
checks.note: Defensibly RIGHT under the Bronsted-Lowry definition taught in high-school chemistry: every acid-base reaction goes to the weaker acid and weaker base ('Equilibrium in acid-base reactions always favors the weaker side'; 'The weaker acid and the weaker base are always on the same side'). Here the products are water (a far weaker acid than HCl) and chloride ion (a far weaker base than hydroxide), so a chemist could call this choice correct. FIX: replace it with the misconception it was meant to carry (facts.md F16): 'The same acid and base, only watered down'.

checks.claim: Context: H+ ions join OH- ions as water; Na+ and Cl- remain as sodium chloride (table salt) dissolved
Context: every such ionic product is called a salt, and each acid and base gives its own
checks.note: e.g. H2SO4 + 2NaOH -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O.

checks.claim: Set-up: boiled water under oil (no air); dry air over calcium chloride (no water); plain water open to air
checks.note: RSC practical: boiled water with a layer of oil to keep air out; sealed tube with calcium chloride to absorb moisture; water open to air.

checks.claim: Only the nail in plain water open to air rusts
checks.note: RSC: the boiled-water/oil and calcium chloride nails do not rust; 'water and air (actually oxygen in the air) are essential for rusting'.

checks.claim: Key: the first tube rules out that water without oxygen can rust iron
checks.note: Grokipedia: rust needs 'both moisture and dissolved oxygen'; corrosion far slower in deaerated water.

checks.claim: Wrong: oxygen without water (that is ruled out by the dry tube, not the first)
checks.note: 'dry iron does not rust'; the dry tube is the one that tests it, so this is wrong for 'the first tube'.

checks.claim: Wrong: water and oxygen together rust iron (not ruled out; the third tube shows it)
Wrong: iron needs salt in the water (plain water rusted it); context: salt makes it rust faster
checks.note: RSC: 'Salt can increase the rate of rusting'; Grokipedia: NaCl increases corrosion rates.

checks.claim: A 10 C rise roughly doubles the rate of many reactions
checks.note: OpenStax, chemguide and Grokipedia Collision_theory all give it as a rough rule for many reactions; the stem says 'many' and 'roughly'.

checks.claim: From 20 to 30 C gas collision frequency rises less than 2 percent
checks.note: Chemguide: frequency goes as the square root of kelvin temperature, 293 K to 303 K = about 1.7%.

checks.claim: Key: many more collisions are energetic enough to react (at or above the activation energy)
checks.note: Chemguide: the main effect is the large increase in particles with energy at or above the activation energy; Grokipedia: fraction of collisions above Ea rises.

checks.claim: Wrong: the energy a collision needs becomes smaller (activation energy unchanged by warming)
checks.note: Ea is treated as a fixed barrier; temperature acts through the exponential term. Context's 'only a catalyst offers a lower one' is a fair 9th-grade statement (a catalyst gives a lower-Ea route, chemguide); optional softening: 'a catalyst is what offers a lower one'.

checks.claim: Wrong: particles swell up / break into smaller pieces
checks.note: Documented student misconceptions (particles expand when heated); not what happens.

checks.claim: Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee died in a fire in Apollo 1 during a launch-pad test, January 1967
checks.note: 27 January 1967, plugs-out test at Launch Complex 34. Telling is plain and respectful.

checks.claim: Cabin of pure oxygen a little above outside air pressure
checks.note: 'pure oxygen at 16.7 psi (115 kPa), 2 psi (14 kPa) higher than atmospheric pressure'.

checks.claim: Most likely an electrical spark (arc) started it; nylon and foam burned
checks.note: Board: 'The most probable initiator was an electrical arc'; interim report and Grokipedia name nylon and polyurethane foam among the combustibles.

checks.claim: Flames filled the cabin within half a minute
checks.note: Board report: first verbal report 23:31:04.7 GMT, rupture about 23:31:19, fire spread through the crew compartment from about 23:31:25, atmosphere lethal by about 23:31:30, i.e. within about 25-35 s of ignition.

checks.claim: Air is about one-fifth oxygen
checks.note: OpenStax: air 'is only about 20% oxygen'.

checks.claim: Key: more oxygen molecules strike the fuel every second (higher concentration, more collisions)
checks.note: Collision frequency is proportional to concentration; OpenStax: phosphorus burns much faster in pure oxygen than in air.

checks.claim: Wrong: oxygen itself burns as a second fuel
checks.note: Oxygen is an oxidizer, not a fuel.

checks.claim: Wrong: oxygen molecules move faster than nitrogen ones (context: a little slower)
checks.note: Same average KE at the same temperature; O2 (32) is heavier than N2 (28), so about 486 vs 519 m/s at 303 K.

checks.claim: Wrong: oxygen acts as a catalyst (it is used up, so it is a reactant)
checks.note: A catalyst is chemically unchanged at the end; oxygen is consumed in combustion.

checks.claim: Context: pure oxygen has about five times as many oxygen molecules per litre as air
checks.note: Arithmetic: 1/0.21 = 4.8 at equal pressure; 16.7/(14.7 x 0.21) = 5.4 at the test pressure. 'About five' holds either way.

checks.claim: Context: NASA afterwards launched crews in 60 percent oxygen, 40 percent nitrogen
checks.note: Block II launch atmosphere '60% oxygen and 40% nitrogen' at 14.7 psi, vented to 5 psi pure oxygen in flight. True of the Apollo crews that followed (the later Shuttle used ordinary air).

checks.claim: A thick log smoulders slowly; sawdust in a cloud can burn so fast it explodes
checks.note: OpenStax: large pieces of wood smolder, sawdust burns explosively.

checks.claim: Washburn A Mill, Minneapolis: a spark lit airborne flour dust on 2 May 1878
checks.note: 'On May 2, 1878, a spark ignited airborne flour dust within the mill.' MNopedia: spark from two millstones running dry, about 7 p.m.

checks.claim: The blast and fire killed 18 people
checks.note: All 14 of the A Mill's night crew killed; the fire spread to the Diamond and Humboldt mills, which also exploded, killing 4 more: 18 in all (Wikipedia Dust_explosion and Grokipedia Dust_explosion also give 18).

checks.claim: Key: dust specks give far more surface for the air to reach
checks.note: 'Since burning can only occur at the surface of a solid or liquid, where it can react with oxygen, this causes dust to be much more flammable than bulk materials.'

checks.claim: Wrong: richer fuel / smaller molecules (same substance, same molecules)
checks.note: Fineness changes surface area and dispersion, not the substance.

checks.claim: Wrong: specks rub together and grow hot as they fly
checks.note: Not the mechanism; ignition needs an outside source (a spark), and the rate comes from surface area.

checks.claim: Context: 1 kg solid goes from a few hundredths of a square metre to more than a hundred
checks.note: Wikipedia: 1 kg sphere (density 1 g/cm3) 0.048 m2; as 50 micrometre particles (about flour size) about 120 m2.

checks.claim: Context: most deaths come from a second blast of dust shaken up by the first
checks.note: 'Historically, fatalities from dust explosions have largely been the result of secondary dust explosions.'

checks.claim: Hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen on its own, very slowly
checks.note: Slow under ambient conditions (below 1% a year when properly stored); exothermic; gives water and oxygen.

checks.claim: Black manganese dioxide powder makes it froth with oxygen within seconds
checks.note: MnO2 'an effective heterogeneous catalyst', not consumed; chemguide uses MnO2 on H2O2 as its example.

checks.claim: Key: less powder left afterwards would show it is a reactant (reactants are used up; catalysts are not)
checks.note: 'A catalyst is a substance which speeds up a reaction, but is chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction.'

checks.claim: Wrong choices fit either a catalyst or a reactant: frothing ends when peroxide runs out; more powder froths faster; the flask warms
checks.note: Ending when peroxide is gone and warming (exothermic decomposition) happen either way; more catalyst surface or more reactant both speed it. None shows a reactant.

checks.claim: Context: filtered, washed and dried MnO2 weighs what it did before and works again
checks.note: 'Filter the manganese(IV) oxide out ... then wash, dry, and weigh it. Its mass is still 1 g, which shows it hasn't been used up.'

checks.claim: Context: catalase, an enzyme in blood and liver, speeds the same breakdown
checks.note: Catalyses H2O2 decomposition; 'particularly elevated in the liver and erythrocytes' (red blood cells).

checks.claim: Context: platinum, palladium and rhodium in a catalytic converter clean exhaust without being used up
checks.note: 'coated with precious metals such as platinum, palladium, and rhodium'; act 'without being consumed'; CO, hydrocarbons and NOx to CO2, water and N2.

unit_notes: 8 ok, 1 error, 0 uncertain. The one error is a wrong choice true under another definition: Q 69fa384613's 'A weaker acid and a weaker base' is the Bronsted-Lowry description of every acid-base reaction (water and chloride are weaker than HCl and hydroxide); replace it with 'The same acid and base, only watered down'. Optional polish only (not errors): fad0aa3fe0 could mention the two solid boosters beside the three main engines; 142cebecce context's 'only a catalyst offers a lower one' could read 'a catalyst is what offers a lower one'. Apollo 1 and Washburn A Mill facts check against the NASA review board report, Wikipedia, Grokipedia and MNopedia (Washburn A Mill has no Grokipedia page; Wikipedia and MNopedia used).
